job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Hassan Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I finished a computer science degree at Leicester in June, and since September I've been a junior backend developer at a freight firm in Coventry. I build the code that tells drivers which depot to go to next, and I use an AI coding assistant for most of my first drafts. I share a house with two lads from uni, and my mum, who works at a pharmacy counter, makes me take food home on Sundays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like shipping something on Tuesday and watching drivers use it by Wednesday. What wears me out is on-call weeks, when my phone goes off at 3 a.m. and I'm the only junior who knows the route service. I owe about 21,000 and I've got about two months of spending saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, great, I'll keep doing what I do. The tools I use already save me a couple of hours a day, and if they stop at that, I'm still ahead of friends who don't use them. I'd also say it's not hype for me, but it is for plenty of people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a bit let down. I enjoy being close to the new thing, and I'd like the tools to keep getting better. My job feels safe though, and freight isn't going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my day job and put more time into my side project, a small app that helps independent couriers plan their routes. I'd aim to get fifty paying users in a year. And I'd put 250 a month on the loan, because it's my only real debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. A bit restless, because I like it when things move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the side project doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've spent a hundred evenings learning to launch something, which is worth a lot on a CV. I've got a rule that I spend no more than 20 a month on it, so it can't hurt me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who helps with the side project?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mate Dev, who does the design, and my mum, who tests it by being very confused. My mum is the best tester I've got, because she'll tell me straight if a button makes no sense.

say: I'd say the tools already save me **a couple of hours** a day, and I'm ahead of friends who don't use them.
I'd tell friends to build a **side project**.
think: Privately I'm a bit **let down**, because I like being close to the new thing.
My job feels safe because freight **isn't going anywhere**.
do: Aim for **fifty paying users** of my courier route app within a year.
Put **250 a month** on the loan and spend no more than 20 a month on the app.
feel: Pretty good, but a bit **restless** because I like it when things move.
S0.quote: My mum is the best tester I've got, because she'll tell me straight if a button makes no sense.
fieldNote: He treats a quiet world as a **missed opportunity**, not a relief, which shows his adaptive streak.
His low-cost side project rule, 20 a month, shows a careful side under the risk-taking.
His mum is a **practical anchor**, even as a tester.

steps.text: Keep building the freight route service at work
Launch the courier route planner and aim for fifty paying users
Put 250 a month towards the student loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news if you can use it, and a problem if you can't. At work, I'd tell the other juniors to learn the assistant properly and not only for copy-paste. I'd say fewer people will be needed per team, but the ones who can direct it will be worth more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's a bit scary. The card names coding, and that's what I do. My boss told me he used to need six developers for this and could do with four. But I'm the kind of person who gets better each time the tools get better, so I think I'm more likely to be kept than the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd speed up. I'd learn to design whole systems, not just write functions, because that's the human layer. I'd also ask my boss to let me lead one small project, and I'd go deeper on my side app, using AI to build features much faster than a person alone could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit excited. It feels like the early days of something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you're wrong and you're not one of the ones kept?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the side app is my parachute. It won't pay my rent in a year, but with two months of savings and a tiny income I could last a few extra months and find something else. I don't like being fully dependent on one employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you tell your boss about the side project?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in detail. It's on my own time and my own laptop, but I'd tell him if it ever got big, because I'd rather be honest than be found out.

I'd tell other juniors to learn the assistant **properly**.
think: The card names **coding**, and that's what I do; my boss used to need six developers and needs four.
I'm more likely to be **kept** than the rest.
do: Learn to design **whole systems**, not just functions, and lead one small project.
Build the side app faster so it works as my **parachute**.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit excited, like the early days of something.
S1.quote: I don't like being fully dependent on one employer.
fieldNote: He sees the **threat to coding** clearly and still expects to be among the people kept.
His side app is a **hedge**, kept on his own time and laptop.
He'd tell his boss if it grew, a small honesty point.

steps.text: Learn to design whole systems, not only functions
Ask my boss to let me lead one small project
Add AI-built features to the courier route app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast, and I'd want the people who build the tools to be loud about what they're doing. I'd probably write something online about it and see who responds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm anxious, not panicked. AI that does almost any thinking job means my job goes, whatever I do. But I'd be one of the people who knows how the tools work, so I'd have a head start on others. The robots take three more years, so freight drivers and warehouse people have a bit longer than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on my side business and any way to own something. I'd cut spending to the minimum and push my savings to six months. I'd also sit down with my parents and ask what they'd need from me if I lose income, because I'd want to be able to help my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, quick-thinking. It's a rush, to be honest, and I don't love that I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you like it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because change makes me feel awake. But the part I don't like is that I'm 22, my mum's on a pharmacy wage, and my brother is still at school. The bad version isn't only about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your younger brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my brother not to copy my degree, to learn to talk to people and fix things with his hands. It's a weird thing to say after three years of coding, but I'd say it.

say: I'd say two years is **too fast** and tool builders should be loud about what they're doing.
I'd write something online and see **who responds**.
think: AI that does almost any thinking job means my **job goes** whatever I do.
Knowing how the tools work gives me a **head start**.
do: Go all in on my **side business** and push savings to six months.
Ask my parents what they'd need if **I lose income**.
feel: **Anxious** and quick-thinking; it's a rush, and I don't love that I like it.
S2.quote: I'd tell my brother not to copy my degree, to learn to talk to people and fix things with his hands.
fieldNote: He admits to a **thrill** in the change and worries about his family's money, not his own.
His advice to his younger brother is surprising: **learn hands-on skills**.
Mood is anxious because he expects his job to go but has a plan.

steps.text: Put every spare hour into the courier route business
Cut spending to the minimum, starting with takeaways
Build six months of savings in the next year
Sit down with my parents about money if my income stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is the sweet spot where you can still act. I'd tell people to start learning now, and I'd push my company to put a plan in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fairly excited. By 2031 I'll be 27, and if I've built a business or a deep skill by then, I'll be in a good position. The five years also give the three-year robot gap a time to matter, so I could build tools for physical work like freight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim at building tools for logistics, since freight needs both thinking and physical work. I'd grow my side app into a real product, get one or two customers, and save for a deposit with my mate. And I'd keep my day job until the side income was half my salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited with a side of nerves. Five years is just enough to try something big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the side income half your salary a good line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At half, I can survive losing the job. At less than that I'm still at risk. It's a rule of thumb I made up, but I'd stick to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the AI makes your app obsolete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd build something on top of whatever replaced it. The app is mostly knowing what independent couriers actually struggle with, and the AI doesn't know that yet.

say: I'd say five years is the **sweet spot** where you can still act.
I'd push my company to put a **plan in writing**.
think: By 2031 I'll be 27 and, with a business or deep skill, in a **good position**.
The three-year robot gap means I could build **tools for physical work**.
do: Grow the app into a real product with **one or two customers**.
Keep my day job until side income is **half my salary**.
feel: **Excited** with a side of nerves; five years is just enough to try something big.
S3.quote: At half, I can survive losing the job. At less than that I'm still at risk.
fieldNote: He sets a clear **line**, half his salary, before he leaves the job.
His edge is knowing what couriers actually **struggle with**, a human detail.
Excited and nervous at once, which fits his adaptive style.

steps.text: Sign one or two paying courier customers in the next year
Spend 20 hours a month building the route product
Save a deposit with my mate while the job lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and I'd treat it as a gift. I'd tell people to get good at the tools now, because that's what compounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm not worried. By 2036 I'll be 32, and I'd have had time to build a career, a business or both. I think the people who start early win in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work for two more years, then go part-time or leave to run my own thing if the app is growing. I'd put 400 a month into savings and buy a small place with my girlfriend if we get there. I'd keep learning every new tool the week it comes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. I could see the next ten years being good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make it go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I got lazy, or if the economy didn't share any of the gains. I'm centre on most things, but I'd hate to see a few firms take everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do something about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd vote for whoever wants a fair deal, and I'd put some of my own money into small local firms. It's not much, but it's what I can do.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**, and the people who get good at tools now will gain.
I'd tell people that using the tools **compounds** over time.
think: By 2036 I'll be 32 with a career, a **business** or both.
I'm calm, but I'd hate to see a **few firms** take everything.
do: Work two more years, then go **part-time** or leave if the app is growing.
Put **400 a month** into savings and learn every new tool the week it comes out.
feel: **Calm** and curious; the next ten years could be good for me.
S4.quote: I'm centre on most things, but I'd hate to see a few firms take everything.
fieldNote: He is **calm** because he has skills, a side app and time, and he knows it.
His one worry is the **concentration of gains**, not his own job.
He would act through voting and small local investing.

steps.text: Work two more years, then go part-time if the app is growing
Try every new AI tool in the week it launches
Grow the courier app into a real business

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years, no question. In that one my job goes before I've paid off the loan and before my family has any plan, and I'd be rushing everything. What would help is a real income floor, honest information from the people building the tools, and time to move into something that lasts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I know I sound like someone who's already ahead. I'd like to say that being ahead of other people isn't the same as being safe.

headlineQuote: Being ahead of other people isn't the same as being safe.
portrait: Hassan is a 22-year-old **computer science graduate** in his first job as a backend developer at a Coventry freight firm.
He is adaptive, uses an **AI assistant** every day, and runs a side app for independent couriers.
His centre outlook means he wants fair shares for everyone without leaning on a party; his **family** is his main worry.
He moves from restless calm at the plateau to quick **anxiety** at two years, then back to calm at ten.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries him most, because his job would go before the loan is paid and his family has any plan.
whatWouldHelp: A real **income floor**, honest information from the people building the tools, and time to move into something lasting.
